'''''Carduus acanthoides''''', known as the '''spiny plumeless thistle''', '''welted thistle''', or '''plumeless thistle''', is a [[biennial plant]] species of [[thistle]] in the family [[Asteraceae]]. The plant is native to [[Europe]] and [[Asia]] and introduced in many other areas, where it is sometimes considered an [[invasive species]].

==Description==
''Carduus acanthoides'' may exceed {{convert|2|m|ft}} in height and can form weedy monotypic stands. The stem and foliage are spiny and sometimes woolly. The [[specific epithet]] ''acanthoides'' refers to its spiny foliage.<ref name=wisflora/> The plant starts from a flat, basal rosette and then bolts an erect stem with occasional toothed, wrinkled, spiny leaves.<ref name=calipc/> The leaves are {{cvt|4–8|in|cm}} long with lobed or pinnately-divided edges.<ref name=nps/><ref name=wisflora/> The abaxial surface (underside) of the leaf is somewhat hairy.<ref name=fotcr2017/>

At the top of each branch of the stem is an [[inflorescence]] of one to several [[Head (botany)|flower heads]], each rounded, covered in spiny [[bract|phyllaries]], and bearing many threadlike, purple or pink [[disc floret]]s. Each flowerhead is around {{cvt|0.5–1|in}} across.<ref name=wisflora/> It flowers throughout the summer and early fall.<ref name=fotcr2017/> The [[achene]]s are 2–3 mm long, four-angled, with faint lengthwise stripes. The fluffy [[Pappus (flower structure)|pappus]] bristles are 11–13 mm long.<ref name=jm1993/> After flowering and setting seed, it dies.<ref name=wisflora/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Carduus acanthoides'' is [[native plant|native]] from France, [[Italy]], and western Turkey; through Russia and [[Kazakhstan]]; to China.<ref name="grin">{{GRIN |accessdate=16 January 2018}}</ref> In its native range the plant is found in open [[grassland]]s and disturbed areas, and in non-native ranges it is a [[weed]] of annual grasslands, roadsides, fields and [[pasture]]s, and disturbed areas.

The plant has introduced broadly across much of North America where it is sometimes considered a [[noxious weed]] or invasive species.<ref name=jm1993/><ref name=calipc/><ref name=usda/> The [[California Department of Food and Agriculture]] has an active program to control known populations.<ref name=calipc/> It spreads through its seeds. Each plant creates around 1,000 seeds.<ref name=rauschert2015/> However, the plant has beneficial impacts on the native  bees in North America.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Russo |first1=Laura |last2=Nichol |first2=Christina |last3=Shea |first3=Katriona |title=Pollinator floral provisioning by a plant invader: quantifying beneficial effects of detrimental species |journal=Diversity and Distributions |date=2016 |volume=22 |issue=1/2 |pages=189–198 |doi=10.1111/ddi.12397 |jstor=24817466 |s2cid=86411284 |issn=1366-9516|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Although first noted in 1962 in the [[Chicago]] region, it has not been seen since 1985.<ref name=fotcr2017/><!--added this because it doesn't look like a big deal in most areas it is known to occur as an introduced species, despite being labeled invasive by some authorities--> In [[Michigan]] and [[Wisconsin]], it does not occur in [[remnant natural area|remnant, native habitats]], but rather those with a history of disturbance, such as railroad right-of-ways, roadsides, and farm fields.<ref name=miflora/><ref name=wisflora/>
